`birdnetR` sits within an ecosystem of tools that cover the full arc from
optional custom training through species detection to post-processing and
validation. This article gives a high-level map of that ecosystem, shows how to
run birdnetR on many files, and how to hand the results to birdnetTools.

## Stage 1: Custom training (optional) with BirdNET-Analyzer

[BirdNET-Analyzer](https://github.com/birdnet-team/BirdNET-Analyzer) is the
upstream desktop and command-line application. For most users it is **not
required**: birdnetR downloads the pre-trained BirdNET models and can run
predictions out of the box.

Consider BirdNET-Analyzer when you need to:

- train a custom species classifier on your own recordings,
- use advanced configuration options not exposed in birdnetR,
- run batch analyses through a graphical interface.

Custom classifiers trained in BirdNET-Analyzer can be loaded in birdnetR with
`birdnet_load_custom()`.

## Stage 2: Species detection with birdnetR

birdnetR wraps the `birdnet` Python package and exposes two model types in R:

- **Acoustic models** detect species in audio files: BirdNET+ V3.0 (the
  default), BirdNET V2.4, Perch v2 and custom classifiers. Load them with
  `birdnet_load()`, `birdnet_load_perch()` or `birdnet_load_custom()`, run them
  with `birdnet_predict()`, and write the results with `birdnet_write()`.
  `birdnet_encode()` returns embeddings instead of species.
- **Geo models** estimate the expected species for a location and week of the
  year. Load them with `birdnet_load(type = "geo")` and run them with
  `birdnet_predict()`.

`as.data.frame()` converts any prediction object to a plain R data frame.

### Processing many files

When you process many audio files, keep the predictions in Python and write
them to disk without converting them to R data frames. A practical pattern is
to loop over meaningful chunks (e.g. one folder per site or one recording day)
and write one output file per chunk:

```{r batch_predict}
library(birdnetR)

model <- birdnet_load()

# Folders of audio recordings, e.g. one folder per site
audio_folders <- list.dirs("recordings", recursive = FALSE)
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)

for (folder in audio_folders) {
  files <- list.files(folder, pattern = "\\.wav$", full.names = TRUE)
  predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files)

  out_file <- file.path("results", paste0(basename(folder), ".csv"))
  birdnet_write(predictions, out_file)
}
```

This keeps memory use constant regardless of total dataset size, because each
iteration replaces the previous prediction object.

`birdnet_predict()` already uses several CPU cores. Set `n_workers` to change
how many. Don't run birdnetR inside `parallel` or `future` workers; see the
[Troubleshoot](Troubleshoot.html) article.

`birdnet_write()` chooses the format from the file extension:

| Format  | Best for | Notes |
|---------|----------|-------|
| CSV     | birdnetTools, quick inspection, other software | Human-readable; largest file size |
| Parquet | Large datasets analysed in R or Python | Columnar; much smaller than CSV |
| NPZ     | NumPy-based pipelines | Compact; requires Python to read |

Parquet is not supported for geo predictions; use CSV or NPZ instead.
`birdnet_write()` also writes embeddings from `birdnet_encode()`.

In CSV files, `start_time` and `end_time` are text in the form
`"HH:MM:SS.cc"` (hours, minutes, seconds and hundredths), e.g. `"00:00:03.00"`.
In the data frame from `as.data.frame()` they are numbers of seconds.

### Reading Parquet files in R

`birdnet_write(predictions, "results.parquet")` writes Parquet files directly
from Python and does not need the `arrow` R package. To **read** Parquet files
back into R (e.g. with `arrow::read_parquet()`), install `arrow`:

```r
install.packages("arrow")
```

On Linux this may require compilation and can take several minutes.

## Stage 3: Post-processing and validation with birdnetTools

[birdnetTools](https://birdnet-team.github.io/birdnetTools/index.html) is a
separate R package designed to work with tabular BirdNET output, the kind
produced by `as.data.frame()` or `birdnet_write()` in birdnetR.

It provides functions for:

- combining outputs from multiple files or recording sessions,
- filtering detections by species, confidence score, date, or time of day,
- visualising temporal detection patterns as heatmaps,
- running an interactive Shiny app to review and label detections,
- calculating species-specific confidence thresholds to achieve a target
  precision.

birdnetTools does not call Python and has no dependency on birdnetR; it works
with any BirdNET-style data frame.

### Handing results to birdnetTools

birdnetR keeps the column names of the Python package: `input`, `start_time`,
`end_time`, `species_name` and `confidence`. The next birdnetTools release
(after 0.1.0) recognises these columns, so you can pass birdnetR output to it
directly.

birdnetTools 0.1.0 and older expect a `filepath` column and the species name
split into `scientific_name` and `common_name`. Add these columns before you
pass the data on. The species name is split at its first underscore:

```{r rename_for_birdnettools}
df <- as.data.frame(predictions)

df$filepath <- df$input
df$scientific_name <- sub("_.*", "", df$species_name)
df$common_name <- sub("^[^_]*_", "", df$species_name)
```

Perch v2 names are scientific names only, so for Perch output both new
columns hold the scientific name.

The same works for results written to CSV files and read back with
`birdnetTools::birdnet_combine()`. Note that the times in CSV files are text
(see above).

## Putting it together

A typical R workflow looks like this:

1. *(Optional)* Train a custom classifier in **BirdNET-Analyzer** and export
   it.
2. Load a model in **birdnetR** with `birdnet_load()`, `birdnet_load_perch()`
   or `birdnet_load_custom()`.
3. Run `birdnet_predict()` on your audio files and save the results with
   `birdnet_write()`.
4. Read the results into **birdnetTools** for filtering, visualisation, and
   validation.

For code examples, see the
[Get started with birdnetR](birdnetR.html) vignette and the
[birdnetTools documentation](https://birdnet-team.github.io/birdnetTools/index.html).
